<reason>Both sides built genuine, competitive cases, but A's line of attack landed more cleanly on the decisive issues. A's physics/certainty framing was never actually refuted, and A successfully turned B's flagship example (the ignition interlock) into a liability by showing incapacitation is inherently reactive — it cannot protect the first victim or any uncaught driver, which B conceded implicitly by shifting to "general deterrence" without fully engaging the split-second decision point A raised. A also neutralized B's most dramatic late move — recasting speed cameras as "penalty machines" — by correctly pointing out the motion targets *post-crash* penalties specifically, not proactive automated enforcement of the design limit itself; B never rebutted this distinction in the closing. B's strongest and most under-answered material was the coverage/scale argument (redesign is slow, capital-intensive, and covers only a fraction of arterial miles) and the sunk-cost economics of existing penalty infrastructure — both real pressure points, but A's answer (cheap, fast interim measures: paint, bollards, humps, cameras) was adequate enough to avoid collapse even if not airtight. B also never engaged A's equity/uneven-enforcement point from the opening. On balance, A more successfully protected its core mechanism claim and neutralized B's best late-round pressure, giving A a clear but not dominant edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's turn on the ignition interlock ("only attaches after a first offense... the pedestrian hit before that first arrest doesn't benefit") combined with A's closing distinction that speed cameras enforce the design limit rather than constituting "post-crash" penalties — this directly defused B's most decisive-seeming late move.</best_rebuttal>
